We have mass spec showing molecular ion m/z 193.1103. That corresponds to formula? Let's compute: C11H13NO2? Let's calculate exact mass: C11 (11*12.0000=132), H13 (13*1.007825=13.1017), N (14.00307), O2 (31.9898) total = 132+13.1017+14.0031+31.9898=191.0946. Not 193. So maybe C11H15NO2: mass = 132 + 15*1.007825=15.1174 +14.0031+31.9898=193.1103 matches observed. So formula C11H15NO2 matches mass spec. Good.

Proton NMR: signals: 1.20 (d, 3H) suggests ethyl CH3 attached to CH (maybe CH-CH3). 2.85 (d, 2H) maybe CH2 next to carbonyl? 3.09 (qdd, 1H) maybe CH attached to CH3 and CH2? 3.81 (s, 3H) methoxy. Aromatic 7.15 (ddd, 2H) and 7.92 (ddd, 2H) typical para-disubstituted anisole? Actually anisole (methoxy phenyl) gives aromatic 6.9-7.2. Here we have two sets of 2H each, suggests para-disubstituted benzene with electron-withdrawing group (C=O) and OMe. So structure: p-methoxybenzamide? But we have N-alkyl chain: C(=O)NCCC? The N attached to propyl? The N-CH2-CH2-CH3? The N-CH2-CH2-CH3 would give CH3 (triplet) not doublet. Observed 1.20 d (3H) suggests CH3 coupled to a CH (quartet). So maybe isopropyl? CH(CH3)2 gives doublet for CH3 (6.5 Hz) and septet for CH. But we have 1.20 d (3H) and 3.09 qdd (1H). That could be CH-CH3 where CH is attached to N and CH2? Actually N-CH-CH3? The CH (1H) shows quartet (coupled to 3H) and also doublet of doublet from coupling to CH2 (2H). So pattern matches N-CH-CH3 with adjacent CH2. So chain: -CH2-CH(CH3)-? Wait N attached to CH2? The N is attached to carbonyl (amide) and to CH2? The SMILES we tried: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)NCCC (N-CH2-CH2-CH3). That would give CH3 triplet, not doublet. So not match.

Alternative: N attached to CH (bearing CH3) and CH2? So N-CH(CH3)-CH2? That would be N-CH(CH3)CH2? The N attached to CH (bearing CH3) and carbonyl. So amide: C(=O)N-CH(CH3)-CH2? That would give CH3 doublet (coupled to CH), CH (quartet) and CH2 (maybe doublet). Observed 2.85 d (2H) could be CH2 adjacent to carbonyl? Actually CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha to carbonyl) appears ~2.5-3.0 as a doublet if coupled to CH. So plausible.

Thus structure: p-methoxybenzamide with N-CH(CH3)CH2? Wait carbonyl attached to N, N attached to CH(CH3)CH2? The chain length: N-CH(CH3)-CH2-? Actually we have only CH2 (2H) and CH (1H) and CH3 (3H). So total 6 H in side chain, matches C3H6? plus N. So side chain is -CH(CH3)CH2- attached to N. So N attached to CH (which is attached to CH3 and CH2). So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N[C@H](C)C? But need CH2 after? Actually CH attached to CH3 and CH2, so CH has one H, attached to CH3 and CH2. So N-CH(CH3)CH2? That CH2 is terminal? It would have 2 H, but no further substituents. So side chain is -CH(CH3)CH2- (propyl with branch). So overall formula: C11H15NO2 matches.

SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N[C@@H](C)C? Wait need CH2 after CH? Actually N-CH(CH3)CH2-? The CH2 is attached to CH (which is attached to N). So chain: N-CH(CH3)-CH2-? The CH2 is terminal, no further atoms. So side chain is -CH(CH3)CH2- (2 carbon atoms). That's isobutyl? Actually isobutyl is -CH2-CH(CH3)2. Not same. Our is 2-carbon chain with branch: CH(CH3)CH2- is 2 carbons, but branch on first carbon. That's 1-methylethyl? Wait CH(CH3)CH2- is same as ethyl with methyl on the carbon attached to N: N-CH(CH3)CH2- (i.e., 2-aminopropyl?). That's 2-aminopropyl but reversed. So SMILES: N[C@@H](C)C? That is N-CH(CH3)CH3 (isopropyl). Not correct.

We need N-CH(CH3)CH2. So SMILES: N[C@@H](C)C? Actually that gives N attached to CH which has CH3 and H and CH3 (two methyls). Not correct.

We need N-CH(CH3)CH2. Represent as N[C@@H](C)C? The second C is CH2? In SMILES, "C" after chiral carbon is CH3 unless specified as "C". To indicate CH2, need "CC". So N[C@@H](C)C? That is N-CH(C)(C) which is isopropyl. For CH(CH3)CH2, we need N[C@@H](C)C? Actually N-CH(CH3)CH2- would be N[C@@H](C)C? The second C is CH2 attached to something else? If terminal, then CH2 attached to nothing else, but SMILES would be "N[C@@H](C)C". That carbon after parentheses is CH3, not CH2. So need "N[C@@H](C)CC"? That would be N-CH(CH3)CH2CH3 (propyl). Not correct.

We need N-CH(CH3)CH2- (CH2 attached to something else? maybe hydrogen only). In SMILES, terminal CH2 is "C". But carbon with two hydrogens and one bond to previous carbon and one bond to something else (like H). So N-CH(CH3)CH2- would be "N[C@@H](C)C". Wait the carbon after is CH2 attached to the chiral carbon and has two hydrogens, that's "C". So "N[C@@H](C)C" indeed is N-CH(CH3)CH2. Because the first C after N is chiral carbon with attached CH3 (branch) and attached to next carbon "C" which is CH2. So correct.

Thus full SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N[C@@H](C)C

Check formula: Let's compute: aromatic ring C6H4 (since two substituents). Add OMe: OCH3 adds C1H3O1. Add carbonyl C=O adds C1O1. Add amide N adds N1. Side chain: CH (C1H1) + CH3 (C1H3) + CH2 (C1H2). Total carbons: 6+1+1+1+1+1 =11. Hydrogens: ring 4 +3+? carbonyl none + side chain 1+3+2 =13? Wait need total H15. Let's count: aromatic ring C6H4 (since two substituents replace two H). OMe adds 3 H. Side chain: CH (1 H), CH3 (3 H), CH2 (2 H). That's 4+3+1+3+2 =13. Missing 2 H maybe on amide N? N has H? In our SMILES N attached to carbonyl and chiral carbon, no H. But amide could have H? The observed N-H maybe not present. The formula we need C11H15NO2 includes 15 H. Our count 13. So we need two more H, likely N-H (1) and maybe extra H on aromatic? But aromatic already accounted. Actually OMe adds 3, side chain 6, ring 4 =13. Need 2 more: N-H (1) and maybe carbonyl carbon attached to O? No. So maybe side chain is CH(CH3)CH2CH3? That adds extra CH3 (3 H) making total 16? Not.

Alternative: side chain could be CH2-CH(CH3) (i.e., N-CH2-CH(CH3) ), which would give CH2 (2H) and CH (1H) and CH3 (3H) =6 H same as before. Still 13 total.

Thus need N-H present: add 1 H gives 14. Still missing 1. Maybe aromatic ring has 5 H (monosubstituted) but we have para-disubstituted, so 4 H. So maybe OMe not present? But OMe is needed for aromatic pattern? Could be anisole pattern with 4 H.

Thus maybe formula C11H15NO2 includes N-H and maybe extra H on carbonyl? Not.

Let's compute exact mass of C11H15NO2: 193.1103 matches. So our SMILES must give that formula. Let's compute formula of COc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N[C@@H](C)C using tool.
